rationale: Start with a broad gradient at intermediate temperature to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. This provides a baseline for testing slope and temperature selectivity.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty and measure how the closest pairs respond to slope. The initial run has substantial resolution margin and all compounds elute well below the final organic fraction.

Test temperature selectivity at the faster gradient while keeping its slope unchanged. Higher temperature should shorten retention and may separate the critical cluster enough to retain the zero time penalty.
Test the midpoint temperature to balance the critical cluster at 40 C against the different co-eluting pair at 60 C. This keeps the fast gradient and should retain the zero time penalty.

Probe 55 C, where the late critical pair should improve before the earlier pair reaches its co-elution at 60 C. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates this selectivity tradeoff without adding a time penalty.

Slightly flatten the gradient at the best temperature to improve the early critical pair and test the response of the later pair. The current last-peak time leaves room for a modest increase in gradient duration without a time penalty.

Injection 6 already achieved the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Slightly lower phi1 to test whether a shallower gradient improves the resolution margin while keeping the last peak within the zero-penalty time window.

The maximum CRF is already secured by injection 6. Test a slightly higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention and probe critical-pair selectivity, while checking that the first peak remains adequately retained.

Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 8 to improve its early critical pair while preserving the later pair’s resolution margin. This may recover the maximum CRF with a shorter last-peak time than injection 6.
